newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rejects request for US agents to carry guns.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rejects request for US agents to carry guns.

text.p: Mexico has rejected a request by Washington to allow U.S. anti-drug agents to carry weapons in Mexico, a top Mexican official said on Wednesday.
Juan Rebolledo, Mexico's deputy foreign minister, said the topic was discussed during two days of high-level meetings between Mexican and the U.S. officials in Mexico City on Monday and Tuesday.
The meeting came amid recriminations between the two nations over the U.S. "certification" of Mexico as an aid-worthy ally in the war on drugs.
The U.S. Congress is seeking to overturn President Bill Clinton's ruling, charging that Mexico is failing to hold up its end, largely because of high-level corruption.
Rebolledo insisted that an anti-drug working agreement between the two countries "is for intelligence exclusively."
"There is nothing here to authoriize an (armed) operation of any type," Rebolledo said in a live interview on Radio Red.

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has been seeking Mexican permission to allow its agents to carry guns in Mexico, but it is a sensitive issue for Mexicans who are concerned about sovereignty and wary about appearing to cave in to the power to the north.
This week's meetings were the latest in a series between Mexican and U.S. officials over the past two years on bilateral legal issues, concentrating on the war on drugs.

The two sides agreed to expedite extraditions of criminals, which the Mexican media portrayed as a Mexican agreement to send any top drug lords who are captured here to the United States for prosecution. Rebolledo disputed that interpretation but he underscored the importance of moving wanted criminals across the border when needed.
"It's important that these extraditions be fast and efficient and in accordance with the law," Rebolledo said. "There is a natural demand to avoid impunity in one country or another."

In 1996, Mexican authorities immediately sent captured drug boss Juan Garcia Abrego to the United States for prosecution, drawing nationalist protests. But Garcia Abrego, who headed the Gulf cartel on the Texas-Mexico border, was a U.S. citizen. He later was convicted and sentenced to life in a U.S. federal court in Houston.

The Foreign Ministry said in a statement that, in addition to speeding extraditions, the two sides will step up cooperation on returning stolen cars that are spirited across the border, crack down on illegal arms smuggling, work closer to stop money laundering and strengthen a bilateral intelligence group with more equipment and personnel.
